Thermal/heat transfer and Slosh models: Heat transfer and sloshing analyses were performed on the Phase 1 (cylindrical tank) to be tested at the end of Phase 1, to determine the requirements for insulation, vacuum and assess boil-off rate. Additionally, a sloshing analysis was performed for a preliminary assessment of the degree of slosh mitigation from baffles. 3.1. Heat leak and Boil-off computations for Phase 1 tank: Heat transfer modeling focused on evaluating the thermal response of the Phase I prototype under cryogenic conditions. The goal was to estimate the boil-off rates for increasing quantities of LH2 in the tank. The analysis shows that the smaller first prototype will have a greater boil-off loss due to its smaller volume and greater surface area to volume ratio. Figure 15 shows the trend between thermal loss or boil-off and tank size for a cylindrical tank. In this analysis, heat leak into the tank is calculated based on tank surface area and insulation characteristics for typical MLI insulation. The heat leak is then translated into an evaporation mass flow rate based on the latent heat of vaporization for LH2. The figure also shows that for the Phase I tank, the boil-off will be around 2% per day due to its small size. Since heat leak (i.e., boil off mass) is proportional to surface area, for larger tanks (i.e. Phase II tank and a full-sized tank for a semi-truck), boil off as a percentage of tank capacity will be significantly lower and potentially below the 1% per day limit. While this simplified analysis captures only losses through the insulation, high-fidelity models capturing structural details have also been developed (Figure 16). Simulations show that inner tank structural supports can create significant conduction paths and require special care to minimize thermal losses. Inter-tank supports: Inter-tank structural supports are components placed between the inner tank and the outer tank. They support the weight of the inner tank with liq. H2, through contact with the outside tank. These loads get reacted out of the outer tank and into the truck structure to which the tank is attached. However, these inter-tank supports also serve a path for heat ingress into the inner tank. Detailed simulations show that inter-tank structural supports can create significant conduction paths from the outer tank to the inner tank, and will require innovative solutions and optimization to minimize thermal losses while providing the required mechanical support.
